source.authors: Caroline M. F. Durif, Daniel Nyqvist, Bastien Taormina, Steven D. Shema, Anne Berit Skiftesvik, Florian Freytet, Howard I. Browman
source.title: Magnetic fields generated by submarine power cables have a negligible effect on the swimming behavior of Atlantic lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) juveniles

value: no effect of the coil-generated magnetic field on activity (time swimming relative to stationary pauses) or distance travelled
method: behavioural: juveniles exposed to an artificial static magnetic field from a coil (on) against coil off (control); activity and distance travelled scored
conditions: Hatchery-reared juveniles (eggs from Skaerneset fisk AS, reared at the Austevoll Research Station), 7 months old, 8 +/- 1 cm; 24 fish per treatment (48 in all). Coil on (static DC field reaching 230 uT, measured along the central axis with a smartphone magnetometer and also estimated by B = 0.2 I/d; the Discussion says up to 220 uT) against coil off as control, inside a raceway; ambient geomagnetic field 51 uT; treatment (n = 6) and control trials (n = 6) were alternated, not randomised. Swimming speed tested with a linear mixed-effects model (fish as random intercept, likelihood-ratio test), speeds below 0.5 cm/s dropped to remove immobile fish. The 16% reduction is the abstract's figure; a per-trial effect size and P value were not read.
quote: Juvenile lumpfish activity, defined as the time that the fish spent swimming relative to stationary pauses (attached to the substrate), and the distance travelled, were unaffected by exposure to the artificial MF.
note: Null result for activity and distance travelled. Sentence returned in two abutting pieces by the page tool (said in pieces). Family and order from OBIS (accepted Cyclopterus lumpus (Linnaeus, 1758), Cyclopteridae, Perciformes); not printed on the page. Licence: page prints 'Creative Commons Attribution License'; Crossref CC BY 4.0, content-version unspecified. Authors as Crossref (page shows only 'Durif et al.' in the text read). Companion record: swimming speed was reduced. Earlier held in desk-d224 for the quote; the abstract sentence is under 40 words.

quote: The swimming speed of juvenile lumpfish was reduced (by 16%) when the coil was on indicating that the fish could either sense the MF or the induced electric field created by the movement of the fish through the magnetic field.

source.authors: Lei Bian, Xiao Ming Cai, Zong Xiu Luo, Zhao Qun Li, Zong Mao Chen
source.title: Foliage Intensity is an Important Cue of Habitat Location for Empoasca onukii

method: physiological: electroretinogram (ERG) spectral sensitivity of the whole compound eye
conditions: Laboratory-reared adults 2-4 days old from a colony kept at 25 +/- 2 C and 70 +/- 3% RH (not wild-caught). ERG: dark-adapted 30 min, 100 ms monochromatic flashes 5 s apart from a xenon arc lamp through narrow-band filters; maximum quantum flux of each wavelength adjusted to about 10^11 photons cm-2 s-1 and calibrated with neutral-density filters; recorded five times for each sex, giving ten spectral scans; the number of insects is not stated. Sexes did not differ in spectral sensitivity (p > 0.05), so the peaks are pooled. Nonlinear least-squares fitting of three putative visual pigments gave 356, 435 and 542 nm in the amplitude ratio 1:0.6:6.4 (UV:blue:green), a fit not a measured single-cell peak; the next sentence of the paper begins 'It was difficult to perform unicellular recording', so single-cell recordings were not made.
quote: The spectral sensitivity curves of the compound eye have two major peaks, with the primary peak at 540 nm and a secondary peak at 355 nm (Figure 4).
note: Primary ERG peak of the compound eye. Sentence returned in two abutting pieces (said in pieces); the page's trailing '([Figure 4])' is shown as printed. Family Cicadellidae as printed on the page; order Hemiptera. Licence: page links CC BY 3.0; Crossref CC BY 4.0 vor. ERG peak is a whole-eye sensitivity, not a single pigment lambda max; fitted pigments (356, 435, 542 nm) are in the conditions.

source.authors: Casper J. van der Kooi, Almut Kelber
source.title: Achromatic Cues Are Important for Flower Visibility to Hawkmoths and Other Insects

method: behavioural: two-choice test between a lighter and a darker blue stimulus of the same hue, exact binomial test against equal choice
value: 11 of 12 responding moths chose the brighter (Light Blue) stimulus first; exact binomial p = 0.006
conditions: Two circular blue flower-like paper stimuli of 2 cm diameter, 'Light Blue' and 'Dark Blue', with the same chromatic properties but different intensities (achromatic), offered together in a flight cage; light level measured at the centre of the cage with a Hagner Screen Master; the first probe was the recorded choice and no reward was given (page summary of the Methods). Pupae were bred on the natural larval food plant (Galium sp.) and eclosed in the flight cage; supplier or laboratory culture is not named. Moths that did not approach and probe the display within 5 min of taking flight were excluded (three D. elpenor and four M. stellatarum), so the counts are of responders. The Methods give no number tested overall. The paper is a Hypothesis and Theory article; the choice experiment is its own, alongside a literature synthesis and optical modelling not used here. Stimulus intensity adjusted to 10 lux for D. elpenor (measured). The 12 responders were all that approached; 11 chose Light Blue, 1 Dark Blue.
quote: Of these moths, eleven approached Light Blue first, whereas one chose Dark Blue (p = 0.006, exact binomial test; 99% confidence interval: 0.52–1.00).
note: Sentence returned in two abutting pieces (said in pieces). Family printed in Table 1 only as 'Sphingidae (Lepidoptera)' for the hawkmoth group, no species named in that row; the species-to-family step is the desk's. Licence: Crossref CC BY 4.0, content-version vor; the page text read had no licence sentence. Issue number not printed in the text read.

source.authors: Atsushi Suzuki, Yoichi Sato, Eri Inomata, Yukio Agatsuma, Masakazu N. Aoki, Hikaru Endo
source.title: Light and Substrate Color Preferences in the Marine Isopod Cymodoce japonica
source.journal: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering 14(19): 1858

method: behavioural: time spent in coloured-light compartments (dark, red, green, blue) in paired choice trials
conditions: Two-compartment light choice, one isopod at a time (each experiment conducted 30 times, 30 trials per light pairing), 5 min per trial with presence recorded every minute; the isopod was released at the centre; light at the aquarium bottom set to 15 umol photons m-2 s-1 (a set level; the spectra of the coloured lights are not given in the passages read). Animals wild-caught in April 2018 (200 caught; 30 active individuals of 13.0-20.4 mm used; inactive isopods that did not respond to light in preliminary trials were excluded, so results hold for active animals only). Pairings reported: dark v red, dark v green, dark v blue, red v green, red v blue, green v blue. Trial order and compartment side are not described in the passages read. Likelihood-ratio tests. Substrate-colour experiment (red, orange, yellow, blue straws) is a separate experiment not used here.
value: no difference in time spent between the dark and red-light compartments (likelihood ratio test, p = 0.191)
quote: There was no significant difference between the time isopods spent in the dark and red-light compartments (Figure 5; likelihood ratio test, p = 0.191).
note: Null result. Sentence returned in two abutting pieces (said in pieces). Family and order from OBIS (accepted Cymodoce japonica, Sphaeromatidae, Isopoda); not printed in the passages read.
